summary: The note describes the Rio Grande rift, a north-trending continental rift zone separating the Colorado Plateau from the North American craton, extending from central Colorado to Chihuahua, Mexico. It covers the rift's basins and cross-sections, its geology including the Santa Fe Group sediments and volcanism, notable features such as the Jemez Lineament and Socorro magma body, and the tectonic history of extension since about 35 Ma, along with proposed mechanisms for its formation.
one_line: Overview of the Rio Grande rift, a north-south continental rift zone in the southwestern US and northern Mexico, covering its basins, geology, volcanism and tectonic history.
key_facts: The Rio Grande rift is a north-trending continental rift zone that separates the Colorado Plateau in the west from the interior of the North American craton on the east.
The rift extends from central Colorado in the north to the state of Chihuahua, Mexico, in the south.
The Albuquerque basin is the largest of the three major basins, spanning 160 kilometres (99 mi) north–south and 86 kilometres (53 mi) east–west at its widest points.
The three major basins of the rift, from northernmost to southernmost, are the San Luis, Española, and Albuquerque basins.
The Albuquerque basin contains 7,350 metres (24,110 ft) of Paleogene clastic sediments deposited on Precambrian basement.
Formation of the rift began with significant deformation and faulting with offsets of many kilometers starting about 35 Ma.
Cenozoic extension started about 30 million years ago (Ma), with two phases of extension observed: late Oligocene and middle Miocene.
The Socorro, New Mexico, region hosts an inflating mid-crustal sill-like magma body at a depth of 19 km, responsible for anomalously high earthquake activity.
The largest rift-associated earthquakes in historic times, two events of approximately magnitude 5.8, occurred in July and November 1906 in the Socorro region.
Earth and space-based geodetic measurements indicate ongoing surface uplift above the Socorro magma body at approximately 2 mm/year.
The youngest eruptions in the rift region are in the Valley of Fires, New Mexico, and are approximately 5,400 years old.
The sedimentary fill of the basins is largely known as the Santa Fe Group, which contains sandstones, conglomerates, and volcanics.
The Jemez Lineament intersects the rift in northern New Mexico and extends well into Arizona, defined by aligned volcanic fields and calderas including the Valles Caldera National Preserve.
The Rio Grande follows the course of the rift from southern Colorado to El Paso, where it turns southeast and flows toward the Gulf of Mexico.
One theory holds that the Colorado Plateau acts as a semi-independent microplate that rotated 1-1.5° clockwise relative to the North American craton, creating the rift.
